opus-5.5.text:
I think that's actually one of the things I admire most about Kaiming. For most of us, the mind is very noisy. You read a new paper on arXiv, you see what people are talking about on Twitter, there's a new trend every few weeks, and it's really hard not to get pulled in different directions. I'm definitely like that. My thoughts jump around a lot, I get excited about many things at once.

Kaiming is very different. When I was working with him, what struck me was that he has this almost unusual calm. He doesn't chase the hot topic just because it's hot. He thinks very carefully about what the real problem is, and once he decides something is worth doing, he goes very deep and stays with it for a long time. Even when things don't work at first, he doesn't panic or switch directions immediately. He keeps simplifying, keeps asking, "What is the essential thing here?"

I don't think it's that he doesn't have distracting thoughts. Everyone does. It's more that he has a very clear sense of taste and judgment about what matters, and that acts like a filter. If you know what you care about deeply, a lot of the noise just naturally falls away. You can see this in his work. ResNet, Mask R-CNN, MoCo, MAE: they're all very simple ideas in the end, but getting to that simplicity requires a huge amount of focus and patience.

For me, that's something I'm still learning. I don't think you can just copy his personality, but you can learn the habit of stepping back and asking whether what you're doing is really important, or whether you're just reacting to what's around you. That's probably the biggest lesson I took from working with him.

r001.rationale: The response portrays Kaiming as deciding carefully what matters, then committing deeply and persistently without quickly changing direction, which clearly conveys strong decisiveness.

fable-5.1.text:
Saining Xie: I think that's actually one of the things I admire most about Kaiming. A lot of people in this field, myself included, get pulled in a hundred directions. There's a new paper every day, a new benchmark, a new trend on Twitter, and it's very hard not to react to all of that noise. Kaiming somehow just doesn't. He picks one problem that he believes is fundamentally important, and he stays with it for a long time, even when it's not fashionable.

When we were working together at FAIR, I noticed he's very disciplined about asking "what is the simplest thing that could possibly explain this?" He's not chasing complexity or trying to add more pieces. He would rather strip things away until the core idea is clear. And I think that simplicity is actually what gives him the focus. If your idea is simple, you can hold the whole thing in your head, and you can keep returning to it without getting lost.

The other thing is that he's very comfortable with slowness. He doesn't feel pressure to publish constantly. He'll sit with a question for months. ResNet, MAE, these didn't come from rushing, they came from really understanding why the previous approaches weren't working. I think a lot of us have the ability to think deeply, but we don't give ourselves permission to spend that much time on one thing. He does.

So to me it's less about controlling thoughts and more about taste and patience. He knows what he cares about, and he trusts that if the question is good enough, the answer is worth waiting for. That's something I try to learn from, honestly, and I still find it hard.

r001.rationale: He is described as choosing one important problem and sticking with it despite distractions, showing clear, firm prioritization.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s impressive about Kaiming is that he can hold on to a question for a very long time. It’s not necessarily that he never gets distracted or has unrelated thoughts. It’s that he keeps returning to the thing he thinks really matters.

In research, that’s difficult because there are always new ideas and new results pulling your attention elsewhere. You can be busy every day without really going deeper into a problem. To me, that kind of focus is less about forcing yourself to control every thought and more about having a clear sense of which question deserves your attention—and being willing to stay with it when progress is slow.

r001.rationale: The response describes Kaiming as persistent in returning to an important research question, but does not characterize him as highly decisive.

sol-6.1.text: I think that’s a remarkable ability. It’s easy to say you should stay focused, but in research there are always new ideas and directions competing for your attention. Your thoughts don’t necessarily follow the plan you’ve made. What I admire about Kaiming is the ability to keep returning to the central question: What is the actual problem, and what matters most for solving it? To me, focus doesn’t mean never getting distracted. It means being able to recognize the distraction and bring your attention back.

r001.rationale: The response praises Kaiming’s ability to refocus and identify what matters most, but does not characterize him as highly decisive.
